items.stem: Reaction rate is defined as:
choices: The amount of product formed at equilibrium
The change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time
The number of collisions per second
items.note: Rate = Δconcentration / Δtime (mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹). Measured from a tangent on a concentration–time graph.

items.stem: For a collision between molecules to be successful (a reaction), it must have:
choices: Energy at least equal to the activation energy and correct orientation
items.note: Collision theory: two requirements — E ≥ Eᴀ AND correct orientation. Both together make the small fraction of 'successful' collisions.

items.stem: Which change does NOT increase the rate of a reaction between solutions?
choices: Using larger, single crystals instead of powder
items.note: Larger crystals mean less exposed surface area — slower. Powdering a solid speeds up reactions involving solids.

items.stem: Why does a 10 K temperature rise often approximately double the rate?
choices: Many more molecules gain energy above the activation energy
items.note: The collision frequency rises slightly, but the big effect is on the Maxwell–Boltzmann tail: the fraction of molecules with E ≥ Eᴀ grows disproportionately.

items.stem: On a Maxwell–Boltzmann energy distribution curve, the area under the curve represents:
items.note: Area = number of molecules. A catalyst lowers Eᴀ (line moves left); higher temperature flattens and shifts the curve right, enlarging the tail beyond Eᴀ.

items.stem: A catalyst increases the rate of a reaction by:
choices: Providing an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy
items.note: Lower Eᴀ → more successful collisions. The catalyst is regenerated unchanged, and ΔH is unaffected.

items.stem: Powdered marble reacts faster with acid than a single large piece of the same mass because powdering:
choices: Increases the surface area exposed to collisions
items.note: Same mass, more exposed surface → more collision sites. Nothing about Eᴀ, energy or concentration changes.

items.stem: A dynamic equilibrium can only be established in:
items.note: Closed system: nothing enters or leaves. Forward and reverse rates become equal, concentrations stay constant (not necessarily equal!).

items.stem: At equilibrium, which statement is correct?
choices: Forward and reverse reactions have stopped
Forward and reverse rates are equal
Reactant and product concentrations are equal
The reaction has gone to completion
items.note: Dynamic = both reactions continue at equal rates. 'Equal concentrations' is the classic misconception.

items.stem: For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, the equilibrium constant expression is:
items.note: Products over reactants, each raised to its coefficient. Pure solids and pure liquids are omitted (constant concentration).

items.stem: If K ≫ 1 for a reaction, at equilibrium:
items.note: Large K = product-favoured. K ≪ 1 = reactant-favoured. K's size says nothing about how FAST equilibrium is reached — that's kinetics.

items.stem: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium:
choices: No shift — pressure does not affect gases
items.note: Le Châtelier: higher pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles — 4 → 2, so to the right. Count only gas molecules.

items.stem: The forward reaction of the Haber process is exothermic. Increasing the temperature:
choices: Shifts equilibrium to the right and increases K
Shifts equilibrium to the left and decreases K
Shifts equilibrium right but decreases K
Has no effect on the position
items.note: Added heat is opposed by shifting in the endothermic (reverse) direction → less NH₃, and K itself decreases. Temperature is the only factor that changes K.

items.stem: Adding a catalyst to a system at equilibrium:
choices: Shifts the position to the right
Shifts the position to the left
Has no effect on the position — equilibrium is reached faster
items.note: Catalysts speed BOTH directions equally. Industrial use: not more product, but the same product sooner (Haber's iron catalyst).

items.stem: The Haber process runs at about 450 °C rather than a lower temperature because:
choices: The yield of NH₃ is higher at 450 °C
The rate is faster, even though the yield is lower — a compromise
items.note: Forward reaction is exothermic, so lower T gives higher yield — but unacceptably slow. 450 °C + high pressure + Fe catalyst is the rate/yield compromise.

items.stem: Adding more N₂ to the Haber equilibrium at constant volume causes:
choices: A shift to the right, producing more NH₃
items.note: Le Châtelier: adding a reactant shifts forward to consume it. K stays constant — the position adjusts, the constant doesn't.

items.stem: For a reaction mixture where Q (the reaction quotient) < K, the reaction will:
choices: Shift in the forward direction (forming products)
items.note: Q compares current concentrations with K: Q < K means too few products → forward shift until Q = K.

items.stem: Adding an inert gas (e.g. argon) at constant volume to an equilibrium mixture causes:
choices: A shift to the side with fewer gas moles
A shift to the side with more gas moles
No shift in the position of equilibrium
items.note: Partial pressures of the reacting gases are unchanged at constant volume → no shift. (At constant pressure it's different — the mixture expands.)

items.stem: In industry, ammonia formed in the Haber process is removed by liquefaction. This is done to:
choices: Shift the equilibrium towards more NH₃ formation
items.note: Continuously removing product keeps Q < K → the forward reaction keeps running — the same logic as Le Châtelier, used industrially.

items.stem: Which factor changes the value of the equilibrium constant K?
items.note: Only temperature changes K. Everything else shifts the position by adjusting concentrations — K itself is untouched.

items.stem: Explain, using Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution curves, why a small increase in temperature causes a large increase in reaction rate.
markscheme: Draw/describe two curves: higher T is flatter and shifted right, same area (1)
Eᴀ marked as a vertical line; the shaded tail beyond Eᴀ grows disproportionately with T (1)
Only molecules with E ≥ Eᴀ can react successfully (1)
A small T rise greatly increases the fraction beyond Eᴀ → many more successful collisions per second → large rate increase (1)
items.tactic: The answer lives in the TAIL of the distribution, not the peak. Sketch both curves, mark Eᴀ, shade the tail — then explain in terms of the fraction of molecules.

items.stem: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH = −92 kJ/mol: (a) write the equilibrium constant expression; (b) predict and justify the shift if NH₃ is removed; (c) predict and justify the effect of lowering the temperature.
markscheme: (b) Removing NH₃ makes Q < K → shifts right, forming more NH₃ (1)
(c) Forward reaction is exothermic; lowering T shifts in the exothermic (forward) direction → more NH₃ (1)
(c) K increases as temperature decreases for an exothermic reaction (1)
items.tactic: Le Châtelier answers need two parts every time: the direction AND the reason in terms of opposing the change. ΔH's sign decides temperature effects.
